## List findings in one numbered table, worst first

_high · any_

**Rule.** Put every finding in one table ordered by severity, then by location, with the columns `#`, `Sev`,
`Where`, `Problem` and `Fix`, plus any column the skill needs (`By`, `WCAG`). Keep each cell to one
line. Where the surface renders file links, make `Where` a link to the file at the line. Past
fifteen rows, split it into one table per file or area under a small heading, numbering straight
through.

**Why.** Findings spread across headings and bullets cannot be scanned or compared, and the numbers are
what let the user answer "apply 1 and 4" instead of quoting the report back.

**Incorrect:**

```markdown
### Critical Issues

#### 1. Missing label
- **Location:** src/Form.tsx:12
- **Description:** The email input has no label.
- **Fix:** Add a label element.
```

**Correct:**

```markdown
| # | Sev | Where | Problem | Fix |
| :-: | :-: | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 🔴 | `src/Form.tsx:12` | Email input has no accessible name | Add `<label htmlFor="email">` |
```

## Mark every status with the shared five-mark scale

_high · any_

**Rule.** Mark status with these five and nothing else: 🔴 broken or blocking, 🟡 costs the user and should
be fixed, 🔵 worth tidying, 🟢 nothing found, ⚪ not checked. Map the tool's own severities onto
them once, in the skill, and use the same marks in the verdict, the scorecard and the findings. The
verdict is the worst mark found.

**Why.** When every audit speaks its own dialect (critical, error, serious, warn, note), a reader moving
between reports cannot compare them, and without ⚪ an area that was never checked reads as passed.

**Exceptions.** A score with its own published thresholds, such as a Lighthouse category from 0 to 100, keeps
those thresholds and shows them as 🔴, 🟡 and 🟢.

## Open an audit report with a verdict line that quotes the tool's own summary

_high · any_

**Rule.** Start the report with one blockquote: the verdict for the worst finding, the count at each
severity, and the summary line the script or tool printed, quoted verbatim. Call a result clean
only when the tool's own exit code or summary says so.

**Why.** A report that opens with details makes the reader scroll to learn whether anything is wrong, and a
"looks clean" written from memory instead of from the tool's output is how a failing check ships.

**Incorrect:**

```markdown
## Audit results

I went through the skill and found a few things worth looking at.
```

**Correct:**

```markdown
## 🩺 Skill audit · `react/accessibility-audit`

> 🟡 **Needs work** · 0 errors · 16 warnings · 10 polish
> `0 error(s), 3 warning(s)` · `6 files · 101 body lines · 1116 ≈tokens · 5 references`
```

## Show a scorecard when the audit covers a fixed set of areas

_medium · any_

**Rule.** When the audit checks the same areas on every run (categories, plugins, URLs, checklist sections),
put a table right after the verdict with one row per area: the area, its worst mark and its
counts. The skill fixes the rows and their order; an area that was not checked stays in the table
marked ⚪.

**Why.** Without a scorecard the reader rebuilds the overall picture from the findings list, and a row that
silently disappears hides an area nobody checked.

**Correct:**

```markdown
| Area | Status | Found |
| --- | :-: | --- |
| Frontmatter | 🟢 | — |
| Description & routing | 🟡 | 1 warning |
| Bundled files | ⚪ | no scripts or assets |
```

## Give a detail block only to findings whose fix will not fit the table, at most five

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Below the findings table, add a `### <n> · <mark> <claim>` block with the quoted evidence and a
diff or before/after only for 🔴 and 🟡 findings whose fix does not fit in the `Fix` cell. Write at
most five, choosing the findings that cost the reader most; findings on the same lines share one
block (`### 1–3 · 🟡 …`). Every other fix is written out when it is applied.

**Why.** A diff under every finding makes the report longer than the thing it audits, and the reader gives
up before reaching the findings that matter.

## Close an audit report with what was not checked and the one next step

_medium · any_

**Rule.** End the report with two lines. **Not checked:** what this run could not cover, and the skill or
step that covers it. **Next:** the one action expected from the user, such as the finding numbers
to apply or the command to run. Anything else the reader should know about the run (a fallback,
findings dropped or merged, a cap) goes in a single line just above them.

**Why.** A report that is silent about what it skipped reads as a pass for everything, and one that ends
without a next step leaves the user guessing whether anything was already changed.

**Correct:**

```markdown
**Not checked:** drawing and hotkeys need a live session → run `claude --plugin-dir .`

**Next:** nothing is applied yet. Reply with the numbers to apply (`1 3`) or `all`.
```

## Report a clean run as the heading and one line

_medium · any_

**Rule.** When the audit found nothing, the report is its heading and one 🟢 line carrying the tool's
summary as evidence. Leave out the scorecard, the findings table and any list of checks that
passed.

**Why.** A clean report padded with every check that passed teaches the reader to skim, and they then skim
the next report, the one with a real finding in it.

**Correct:**

```markdown
## 🩺 Marketplace doctor · `szum-tech`

> 🟢 **Clean** · 15 plugins · 0 errors · 0 warnings · `✓ 0 errors  ⚠ 0 warnings`
```

## Write reports in GitHub-flavoured Markdown without HTML

_low · any_

**Rule.** Build the report only from what every surface renders: headings, tables, emoji, blockquotes, bold,
links and fenced code. Leave out HTML such as `<details>` or styled spans, ANSI colour codes, and
diagrams that need a renderer.

**Why.** The same report is read in the desktop app, in a terminal and in a pull-request comment, and HTML
that one of them does not render shows up there as raw tags.
